title: Study Design & Data Ethics
text:
From the 10/28 in-class activity (Day 9)
The design of a study decides which conclusions the data can support, before any code is written.











Design
What happens
Can show causation?
Watch out for




Randomized experiment
Researcher randomly assigns a treatment
Yes, within the sample
Volunteers may not represent everyone; short time frames


Observational, cross-sectional
Measure people once, at one point in time
No (association)
Confounders; self-report errors


Observational, longitudinal
Measure the same people repeatedly over time
No, but shows change within people
Attrition (people drop out, often not at random)


Observational, retrospective
Use records that already exist (sales, gym entries)
No
Records weren’t made to answer this question




Confounding variable: a third variable related to both the predictor and the outcome (e.g. screen time could affect both sleep and GPA)
Before-and-after comparisons with no comparison group can’t separate the change from everything else that changed (season, prices, marketing)

!! Random assignment ≠ random sampling

Random assignment (who gets which treatment) → supports causal conclusions
Random sampling (who is in the study) → supports generalizing to the population
An experiment on volunteers at one company shows cause for those volunteers, but not necessarily for everyone












Method
Good for
Limitation




Survey / self-report
Internal experiences (stress, mood, opinions)
Recall error, social desirability, nonresponse


Interviews / focus groups
How people describe experiences, in their words
Small samples; stigma can cause underreporting


Wearables / tracking
Objective, repeated measures (sleep, steps)
Device errors; only reaches people who own one


Naturally generated records
Large volumes of real behavior, cheap
Not designed for research; missing context


Web scraping / APIs
Public data at scale (prices, posts, sports stats)
Site terms, changing page layouts; users aren’t representative



A data collection plan should name: target population, data source, collection method, measurements with units/scales and timing, and a limitation.




Consent = a meaningful chance to understand what participation involves and to say no. One “Accept all” click isn’t informed consent for every later use.
Purpose shift: using data for a different purpose than people expected (site analytics → targeted housing ads) raises the privacy risk
“Anonymous” isn’t unidentifiable: browsing patterns + IP address + device details, or a wearable device’s daily routine, can act as a fingerprint












Problem
Example
Fix




Leading / loaded
“Don’t you agree the overpriced dining…”
Neutral wording, no opinion words


Double-barreled
Asks about affordability and eating well in one question
One concept per question


Vague
“Do you get enough sleep?”
Ask for a number, with units


No time frame
“How often do you…”
“During the past 7 days…”


Missing options
Only “car” or “bus” for commuting
Exhaustive options, “select all”, “Other”


Overlapping bins
1–2 hrs, 2–3 hrs
Non-overlapping: 1–2, 3–4


Measures the wrong thing
“How much does social media harm you?” when the goal is time spent
Measure the predictor and outcome separately

title: Workflow & Reminders
text:
install.packages("package_name") installs a package once per computer.

Typed in the Console, never in a .qmd (it would reinstall on every render)
package_name is wrapped in quotes

library(package_name) loads a package and goes in every document

!! On this site, every page is its own R session, so each page loads its own packages





From the Day 4 activity, the workflow for every new .qmd:

Open the .Rproj first, so file paths like read_csv("titanic.csv") work without a full path
First chunk: load packages
Second chunk: import the data and give it a name
Meet the data (glimpse(), head(), check for NAs) before wrangling or plotting

Keep one purpose per chunk. Loading packages and importing data are separate chunks.






I want to…
Shortcut




Run the current line or selection
Cmd + Enter


Run the whole current chunk
Cmd + Shift + Enter


Insert a code chunk
Cmd + Option + I


Type the pipe |>
Cmd + Shift + M


Type the assignment arrow <-
Option + -


Render the document
Cmd + Shift + K


See all keyboard shortcuts (overlay)
Option + Shift + K






Chunk options go on the first lines inside a code chunk and start with #|.






TipIn RStudio, chunk options can be easily toggled with the cogwheel icon under each code chunk.









Option
What it does
When I use it




#| eval: false
Shows the code but never runs it
View(), install.packages(), code I only want to display


#| echo: false
Runs the code and shows the output, but hides the code
A finished plot in a report where the reader doesn’t need code


#| include: false
Runs the code but hides both code and output
Setup chunks (loading packages, importing data)


#| warning: false
Hides warnings (the code still runs)
Known, harmless warnings, e.g. geom_smooth() messages


#| message: false
Hides messages, e.g. the startup text from library(tidyverse)
Package loading and read_csv() column-type messages


#| error: true
Keeps rendering even if the chunk errors, and shows the error
Demonstrating a mistake on purpose (see Pitfalls)


#| label: name
Names the chunk
Finding a chunk in the outline; cross-referencing figures





# A tibble: 3 × 2
  drv       n
  <chr> <int>
1 4       103
2 f       106
3 r        25


!! Warnings vs. messages vs. errors:

Message: just information (e.g. which columns read_csv() guessed)
Warning: something worth checking, but the code still ran (e.g. rows removed because of NAs)
Error: the code stopped and there is no result

Hide messages freely. Only hide a warning after reading it once and deciding it’s harmless.



Both store a value: x <- 5 and x = 5 do the same thing.
Convention: use <- for assignment.

It keeps “store this” (<-) visually separate from “is this equal?” (==)
= is still used to name arguments inside a function: mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
= also works for assignment and some people (including my instructor) use it because it’s quicker. Pick one and be consistent.


# assignment: store the result
jan_flights <- flights |> filter(month == 1)

# = names an argument; == checks equality
jan_flights |> summarize(avg_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  avg_delay
      <dbl>
1      10.0






read_csv("titanic.csv") (with an underscore) is the tidyverse version and returns a tibble
read.csv() (with a dot) is base R and returns a plain data frame, so stick with read_csv()
read_csv() also reads straight from a URL, e.g. TidyTuesday data on GitHub

title: Joins & Relational Data
text:
From the 10/21–10/22 in-class activity (Day 7)
A join is a decision about which records belong together, not just a line of code. Before joining, ask:

What does one row represent in each table?
What makes two records a valid match?
After joining, does the result still answer my question? (Check the row count and what one row now means.)








Source: medium.com













Function
Keeps which rows?
Adds columns from y?
Use it to…




left_join(x, y)
All rows in x
Yes
Add lookup info to my starting table


right_join(x, y)
All rows in y
Yes
Same as a left join with x/y swapped


inner_join(x, y)
Only rows that match
Yes
Analyze complete matches only


full_join(x, y)
All rows from both
Yes
Reconcile/audit two sources


semi_join(x, y)
Rows in x with a match
No
Filter x to records that have a match


anti_join(x, y)
Rows in x with no match
No
Find what didn’t match (diagnostics)


intersect(x, y)
Identical rows in both
No (same columns)
Rows shared by two extracts


union(x, y)
Distinct rows in either
No (same columns)
Stack two compatible tables, no duplicates


setdiff(x, y)
Rows in x not in y
No (same columns)
What was added/removed between snapshots




Read x |> left_join(y, by = "id") as “join y to x”: x is the starting population
Always write by = (or join_by()) so dplyr doesn’t silently match on other columns that share a name





counties <- tribble(
  ~county_id, ~county,   ~population,
  101,        "Alder",   10000,
  102,        "Birch",   20000,
  103,        "Cedar",   15000,
  104,        "Dogwood",  8000
)

health <- tribble(
  ~county_id, ~measure,   ~estimate,
  101,        "Diabetes", 10.2,
  102,        "Diabetes", 12.5,
  103,        "Diabetes",  9.8,
  105,        "Diabetes", 14.1   # 105 isn't in counties!
)

programs <- tribble(
  ~program_id, ~county_id, ~program,
  "P01",       101,        "Walking group",
  "P02",       101,        "Nutrition class",
  "P03",       103,        "Walking group",
  "P04",       104,        "Nutrition class",
  "P05",       104,        "Nutrition class"
)












Key
Meaning
Example here




Primary key
Uniquely identifies each row; never repeated, never NA
county_id in counties


Foreign key
Points to a key in another table; may repeat
county_id in programs


Duplicate key
A key value in several rows: fine for a foreign key, a data problem for a primary key
101 appears twice in programs


Surrogate key
An ID made up just to identify records
program_id ("P01")


Natural key
A meaningful attribute that already identifies the thing
A state + county FIPS code



Check that a primary key really is unique. Both of these should return zero rows:

counties |> count(county_id) |> filter(n > 1)

# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: county_id <dbl>, n <int>

counties |> filter(is.na(county_id))

# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: county_id <dbl>, county <chr>, population <dbl>


!! “Unique in this file” doesn’t make it a good key. county names happen to be unique here, but county names repeat across states.










Relationship
Meaning
Example




One-to-one
Each row matches at most one row on the other side
County → one population value


One-to-many
One row can match several rows
County → its programs


Many-to-many
Rows on both sides can match several rows
Students ↔︎ courses



A one-to-many join adds rows: Alder appears twice after joining programs because it has two programs. State what you expect so dplyr can warn you:

counties |>
  left_join(programs, by = "county_id", relationship = "one-to-many")

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  county_id county  population program_id program        
      <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <chr>      <chr>          
1       101 Alder        10000 P01        Walking group  
2       101 Alder        10000 P02        Nutrition class
3       102 Birch        20000 <NA>       <NA>           
4       103 Cedar        15000 P03        Walking group  
5       104 Dogwood       8000 P04        Nutrition class
6       104 Dogwood       8000 P05        Nutrition class






Prediction first: joining health to counties with a left join should keep all four counties, and Dogwood (104) should get NAs because it has no health row.

counties |>
  left_join(health, by = "county_id")

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  county_id county  population measure  estimate
      <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>
1       101 Alder        10000 Diabetes     10.2
2       102 Birch        20000 Diabetes     12.5
3       103 Cedar        15000 Diabetes      9.8
4       104 Dogwood       8000 <NA>         NA  



!! Dogwood’s NA means no estimate, not a diabetes rate of zero
County 105 is dropped because the join starts from counties


# inner join: only Alder, Birch and Cedar have rows in both tables
counties |>
  inner_join(health, by = "county_id")

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  county_id county population measure  estimate
      <dbl> <chr>       <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>
1       101 Alder       10000 Diabetes     10.2
2       102 Birch       20000 Diabetes     12.5
3       103 Cedar       15000 Diabetes      9.8



!! An inner join silently drops unmatched rows. An average after an inner join describes only the matched counties.


# full join: everything from both sides, NAs wherever there's no match
counties |>
  full_join(health, by = "county_id")

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  county_id county  population measure  estimate
      <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>
1       101 Alder        10000 Diabetes     10.2
2       102 Birch        20000 Diabetes     12.5
3       103 Cedar        15000 Diabetes      9.8
4       104 Dogwood       8000 <NA>         NA  
5       105 <NA>            NA Diabetes     14.1






# Which counties HAVE a health estimate?
counties |> semi_join(health, by = "county_id")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  county_id county population
      <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>
1       101 Alder       10000
2       102 Birch       20000
3       103 Cedar       15000

# Which counties are MISSING a health estimate?
counties |> anti_join(health, by = "county_id")

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  county_id county  population
      <dbl> <chr>        <dbl>
1       104 Dogwood       8000

# Which health rows point to a county we don't have?
health |> anti_join(counties, by = "county_id")

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  county_id measure  estimate
      <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>
1       105 Diabetes     14.1


The two anti joins answer different questions, so the order of x and y matters.



Set operations need tables with the same columns and compare entire rows, not a chosen key.

fall <- tribble(
  ~student_id, ~course,
  1, "Data 200",
  2, "Data 200",
  3, "Data 232"
)
spring <- tribble(
  ~student_id, ~course,
  2, "Data 200",
  3, "Data 232",
  4, "Data 200"
)

intersect(fall, spring)  # identical rows in both terms

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  student_id course  
       <dbl> <chr>   
1          2 Data 200
2          3 Data 232

union(fall, spring)      # every distinct row, once

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  student_id course  
       <dbl> <chr>   
1          1 Data 200
2          2 Data 200
3          3 Data 232
4          4 Data 200

setdiff(spring, fall)    # rows new in spring

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  student_id course  
       <dbl> <chr>   
1          4 Data 200


!! intersect() finds identical student-and-course rows. To find students enrolled in both terms regardless of course, compare just the key: fall |> semi_join(spring, by = "student_id").

title: Joins & Relational Data
text:
Set operations need tables with the same columns and compare entire rows, not a chosen key.

fall <- tribble(
  ~student_id, ~course,
  1, "Data 200",
  2, "Data 200",
  3, "Data 232"
)
spring <- tribble(
  ~student_id, ~course,
  2, "Data 200",
  3, "Data 232",
  4, "Data 200"
)

intersect(fall, spring)  # identical rows in both terms

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  student_id course  
       <dbl> <chr>   
1          2 Data 200
2          3 Data 232

union(fall, spring)      # every distinct row, once

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  student_id course  
       <dbl> <chr>   
1          1 Data 200
2          2 Data 200
3          3 Data 232
4          4 Data 200

setdiff(spring, fall)    # rows new in spring

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  student_id course  
       <dbl> <chr>   
1          4 Data 200


!! intersect() finds identical student-and-course rows. To find students enrolled in both terms regardless of course, compare just the key: fall |> semi_join(spring, by = "student_id").

Plots with ggplot2
text:
Every plot starts with the same structure:
ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ...)) +
  geom_*()

aes() maps columns to things you can see (x, y, color, fill, size)
Each layer is added with a + at the end of the line
Pick the geom by the types of variables (more in Choosing a Plot)











Use Case
Function
Variables




Histogram: distribution of one number
geom_histogram()
1 numerical


Boxplot: spread and outliers
geom_boxplot()
1 numerical (+ 1 categorical)


Bar graph: count each category
geom_bar()
1 categorical


Scatterplot: relationship between two numbers
geom_point()
2 numerical


Jittered points: overlapping points spread out
geom_jitter()
2 numerical or 1 cat. + 1 num.


Count plot: point size = number of overlaps
geom_count()
2 discrete (e.g. ratings 1–5)


Trend line through a scatterplot
geom_smooth()
2 numerical


Reference line at a value
geom_vline() / geom_hline()
any


Small multiples: one panel per group
facet_wrap(~ group)
any + 1 categorical





# Histogram: play around with binwidth
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3)
# Boxplot of one variable
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot()
# Bar graph: counts each category for you
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar()
# Boxplot comparing a number across categories
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() # flip so long category names don't overlap






















From the Day 5 EDA activity

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(subtitle = "Blue: straight line (lm). Red: LOESS curve")











Argument
What it does




method = "lm"
Straight line of best fit (a linear model, see Models)


method = "loess"
Flexible curve that follows the local pattern (the default for small data)


se = FALSE
Removes the gray confidence band around the line


formula = y ~ x
Spells out the formula and silences the “using formula” message




!! If the straight line and the curve disagree (like above for big engines), a single straight line is a poor summary
stat_smooth() does the same thing as geom_smooth()




From the Day 8 activity. When values are whole numbers (ratings 1–5), hundreds of points land on the same spot and the plot hides how many there are.
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cyl, y = hwy)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "geom_jitter() + alpha")
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cyl, y = hwy)) +
  geom_count() +
  labs(title = "geom_count()")











geom_jitter(width =, height =) nudges each point a little at random so stacks spread out

!! Jitter only changes where points are drawn, not the data. Set height = 0 when the y values must stay exact

alpha = 0.4 makes points see-through: darker spots = more points
geom_count() keeps points in place and sizes them by count. Downside: people judge areas poorly




From HW1

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mpg$displ), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(mpg$hwy), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 50))









geom_vline(xintercept =) draws a vertical line; geom_hline(yintercept =) draws a horizontal one
mpg$hwy pulls one column out of a data frame as a vector (needed here because the line isn’t inside aes())
scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 50)) sets the axis range. Starting at 0 avoids exaggerating differences

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
From the R4DS Ch. 10 reading and the 10/14 in-class activity (Day 5), using mpg
EDA means looking at the data before building a model. Five questions to work through:








Idea
Question
Go-to tools




Variation
How much do values differ from case to case?
geom_histogram(), sd(), IQR()


Typical values
What’s a reasonable summary of the “middle”?
mean(), median(), summary()


Unusual values
Which cases stand out? Errors, rare cases, or informative?
geom_boxplot(), 1.5 × IQR rule


Covariation
How do two variables change together?
geom_point(), boxplots by group, color =


Patterns & models
Is the trend linear, curved, clustered?
geom_smooth()






ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Highway mpg", y = "Number of cars")








When describing a distribution, cover:

Center: where most values sit (here, two bumps around 17–20 and 26–27 mpg)
Shape: symmetric or skewed? One peak or several? (here: two peaks, slight right skew)
Spread: how far apart values are
Unusual values: anything far from the rest (a couple of cars above 40 mpg)


mpg |>
  summarize(
    mean_hwy = mean(hwy),
    median_hwy = median(hwy),
    sd_hwy = sd(hwy),
    iqr_hwy = IQR(hwy)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  mean_hwy median_hwy sd_hwy iqr_hwy
     <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1     23.4         24   5.95       9













Measure
What it is
Affected by outliers?
Use when…




Mean
Average of all values
Yes, pulled toward them
Data is roughly symmetric


Median
Middle value (50th percentile)
No (resistant)
Data is skewed or has outliers


Standard deviation
Typical distance of values from the mean
Yes
Paired with the mean


IQR
Q3 (75th pct.) − Q1 (25th pct.): the spread of the middle 50%
No (resistant)
Paired with the median




!! Mean far from median is a clue the data is skewed: the mean gets dragged toward the long tail
Same median, different IQR = same center, different spread





A boxplot flags a point as an outlier if it’s more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the box (below Q1 or above Q3).

mpg |>
  mutate(
    lower_limit = quantile(hwy, 0.25) - 1.5 * IQR(hwy),
    upper_limit = quantile(hwy, 0.75) + 1.5 * IQR(hwy)
  ) |>
  filter(hwy < lower_limit | hwy > upper_limit) |>
  select(manufacturer, model, class, hwy)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  manufacturer model      class        hwy
  <chr>        <chr>      <chr>      <int>
1 volkswagen   jetta      compact       44
2 volkswagen   new beetle subcompact    44
3 volkswagen   new beetle subcompact    41



Three cars are outliers, but the boxplot only shows two dots: two of them have the same hwy value, so their points overlap
Before removing an outlier, ask: is it a data entry error, or a real (rare) case? What do the outliers have in common?
!! “Outlier” depends on the comparison group. Split mpg by class and new outliers appear within each class.




One numerical + one categorical: compare distributions across groups.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip()








Two numerical: scatterplot. Describe the relationship with four words:

Direction: positive or negative?
Form: linear or curved?
Strength: weak, moderate, or strong?
Exceptions: which points don’t follow the pattern?


ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point()








Bigger engines get worse highway mileage (negative, slightly curved, moderately strong). Coloring by class explains many exceptions: the 2-seaters have big engines but better mileage than SUVs and pickups with similar engines.



Adding a trend line helps judge form. See Trend Lines for a straight line vs. a LOESS curve on this same plot. If the two disagree, a single straight line hides a real pattern.

title: Site Guide
text:
Publishing Changes
Committing doesn’t publish anything. GitHub serves whatever is in docs/, so the order is render → commit → push.

Render in RStudio: Build → Render Website (or quarto render in the terminal). This rebuilds docs/ and the course PDFs.
Commit in VS Code: Source Control (Cmd + Shift + G) → stage everything, including docs/ and _freeze/ → write a message → Commit.
Push in VS Code: Sync Changes.
Wait about a minute while GitHub rebuilds the site. Watch it under the repo’s Actions tab (“pages build and deployment”), then hard-refresh with Cmd + Shift + R.







Warning



If I edit a .qmd but skip rendering, the live site won’t change, because docs/ still has the old version.



The Render button on a single file only previews that page. It doesn’t rebuild the course PDF.
Save in RStudio before committing: VS Code only sees saved changes.

title: Choosing Plots & Models
text:
From the 10/26 in-class activity (Day 8)
A plot helps you see and communicate a pattern. A model puts a number on a relationship. You don’t need a model every time you make a plot, and you should always plot before you model.


Start with the question, then name the outcome (what I’m trying to understand) and the predictor (what might explain it), and their types.









Outcome
Predictor
First plot to try
Possible model




Numerical
Numerical
Scatterplot (+ trend line)
Linear regression


Numerical
Categorical
Jittered points or boxplots by group, means marked
ANOVA / linear model with a categorical predictor


Categorical
Categorical
Two-way table; bar chart of proportions
Chi-square test


Binary (yes/no)
Numerical
Proportion “yes” across groups; jittered 0/1 points
Logistic regression


Count
Time
Counts over time
A count model (beyond this class)




These are starting points, not rules
!! A scatterplot is the wrong choice when both variables are categorical: every point lands on a few grid spots




Correlation (r) measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two numerical variables, from −1 to 1.

Positive: big x goes with big y. Negative: big x goes with small y
Near 0: little linear relationship, not “no relationship”
!! A U-shaped curve can have r ≈ 0 even though y depends completely on x. Always look at the plot first.


cor(mpg$displ, mpg$hwy)

[1] -0.76602





The fitted line:
\[\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x\]







Term
Meaning




Slope \(b_1\)
Predicted change in y for a one-unit increase in x


Intercept \(b_0\)
Predicted y when x = 0 (often an extrapolation, so not meaningful)


Residual
Observed y − predicted y: the vertical gap between a point and the line





Question: How much does the predicted exam score go up per extra hour of studying?
Pseudocode: plot hours vs. score → fit a line with lm() → read the slope with coef() → interpret it with units.

model_data <- tibble(
  study_hours = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9),
  score       = c(52, 55, 61, 60, 64, 70, 68, 74, 77, 79, 85, 87)
)

fit <- lm(score ~ study_hours, data = model_data) # outcome ~ predictor
coef(fit)

(Intercept) study_hours 
  48.939810    4.147835 



lm() makes the model but prints nothing; save it with <- and use coef() to see the numbers
!! Formula order is outcome ~ predictor (y ~ x)


# predicted values and residuals for each student
model_data |>
  mutate(predicted = fitted(fit), residual = resid(fit)) |>
  head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  study_hours score predicted residual
        <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1           1    52      53.1    -1.09
2           2    55      57.2    -2.24
3           2    61      57.2     3.76
4           3    60      61.4    -1.38


Answer: Each extra hour studied goes with about 4.1 more points, on average. The intercept (48.9) is the predicted score at 0 hours, which is outside the data (the minimum is 1 hour). A positive residual means the student scored above the line.
!! This is association, not causation: these are observational data, and motivation or prior knowledge could drive both study time and scores.




The same lm() works with a categorical predictor. It then compares group means.

scores <- tibble(
  strategy = rep(c("Flashcards", "Practice problems", "Rereading"), each = 12),
  score = c(72, 75, 78, 69, 74, 80, 76, 73, 77, 71, 79, 74,
            78, 82, 85, 80, 76, 88, 83, 81, 79, 86, 84, 80,
            65, 72, 70, 68, 75, 71, 69, 73, 67, 74, 70, 66)
)

ggplot(scores, aes(x = strategy, y = score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18, size = 4, color = "red")







group_fit <- lm(score ~ strategy, data = scores)
coef(group_fit)

              (Intercept) strategyPractice problems         strategyRereading 
                74.833333                  7.000000                 -4.833333 



R picks a reference group (first alphabetically: Flashcards)
Intercept = mean of the reference group
Other coefficients = difference between that group’s mean and the reference group’s mean

e.g. strategyPractice problems = 7: practice problems averaged that many points more than flashcards

Changing the reference group (relevel()) changes how the coefficients are written, not the group means



A one-way ANOVA asks: do the mean outcomes differ across two or more groups? It compares the variation between group means to the variation within groups.

anova(group_fit)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: score
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
strategy   2 849.56  424.78  38.161 2.611e-09 ***
Residuals 33 367.33   11.13                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



A tiny p-value means the group means differ by more than chance would explain
With exactly two groups, ANOVA, a two-sample t-test, and lm() give the same test
!! Lead with the plot, not the table: means alone hide spread, overlap and outliers





When the outcome is yes/no (pass/fail), a straight line can predict impossible probabilities below 0 or above 1. Logistic regression models the probability of “yes” with an S-shaped curve that stays between 0 and 1.
ggplot(data, aes(x = hours, y = passed)) +   # passed is 0 or 1
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, width = 0) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"))
Matching rule of thumb: numerical outcome → linear model; binary outcome → logistic regression.

title: Common Pitfalls & Troubleshooting
text:
# !! one = means "assign" or "name an argument", not "is equal to"
flights |>
  filter(month = 1)

Error in `filter()`:
! We detected a named input.
ℹ This usually means that you've used `=` instead of `==`.
ℹ Did you mean `month == 1`?


dplyr catches this and suggests the fix:

flights |>
  filter(month == 1) |>
  count(month)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  month     n
  <int> <int>
1     1 27004






# !! any missing value makes the whole result NA
flights |>
  summarize(avg_delay = mean(arr_delay))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  avg_delay
      <dbl>
1        NA



# Fix: ignore missing values
flights |>
  summarize(avg_delay = mean(arr_delay, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  avg_delay
      <dbl>
1      6.90






# Keep only flights in January OR February
# !! PRODUCES A BUGGED OUTPUT
flights |>
  filter(month == 1 | 2) |>
  count(month)

# A tibble: 12 × 2
   month     n
   <int> <int>
 1     1 27004
 2     2 24951
 3     3 28834
 4     4 28330
 5     5 28796
 6     6 28243
 7     7 29425
 8     8 29327
 9     9 27574
10    10 28889
11    11 27268
12    12 28135


Error: R treats nonzero numbers in conditional statements as TRUE, so it reads this as “keep rows where month is 1, or TRUE”, which keeps every row.

# Fix 1
flights |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 2) |>
  count(month)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  month     n
  <int> <int>
1     1 27004
2     2 24951

# Fix 2
flights |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 2)) |>
  count(month)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  month     n
  <int> <int>
1     1 27004
2     2 24951






flights |>
  filter(month == 1) |>
  nrow()

[1] 27004

nrow(flights) # unchanged!

[1] 336776


dplyr verbs never change the original data. To keep the result, save it: jan_flights <- flights |> filter(month == 1).



!! From my own Notes #1: filtering to non-face cards before assigning face-card values meant the face-card rule never ran. Think through the order of steps (write pseudocode) before chaining. See the card deck example.




wide <- tibble(id = 1:2, `2022` = c(5, 6), `2023` = c(7, 8))

# !! names_to without quotes: R looks for an object called year (and finds lubridate's year() function)

Each row is one case (a passenger, a flight, a car)
Each column is a variable measured on that case
Tibbles are the tidyverse’s version of a data frame

A dataset is tidy when it follows three rules (more in Tidying):

Each variable is a column; each column is a variable
Each observation is a row; each row is an observation
Each value is a cell; each cell is a single value




Column types determine which operations are possible. For example, you can take the mean() of a number (int, dbl), but not of text (chr).



Type
Means
Example values

<dbl>

<fct>

The pipe means “and then”.

title: Tidying & Reshaping
text:
From the 10/19 in-class activity (Day 6)
Real data rarely arrives tidy. Before reshaping, ask: what should one row represent?





Use Case
Function
Example




Many columns → fewer, longer columns
pivot_longer()
pivot_longer(cols = -id, names_to = "year", values_to = "n")


Many rows → fewer, wider rows
pivot_wider()
pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value)


Does a text value contain a pattern?
str_detect()
filter(str_detect(name, "County"))


Pull a number out of messy text
parse_number()
parse_number("45 minutes") → 45


Replace text that matches a pattern
str_replace()
str_replace(x, "mins", "")


Make text all lowercase
str_to_lower()
str_to_lower("March") → "march"


Create a small table by hand
tribble()
see Joins



!! In pivots, new column names are quoted (names_to = "year"), but existing columns are not (cols = starts_with("F_count"), names_from = measure). This is the exception to dplyr rule 2 in Data Basics.



Use when column names are actually values of a variable (years, seasons, episodes).

# A wide table: one column per year
wide <- tribble(
  ~county,  ~`2021`, ~`2022`, ~`2023`,
  "Alder",  10.1,    10.4,    10.2,
  "Birch",  12.0,    12.3,    12.5
)

wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -county,          # every column except county (unquoted: it exists)
    names_to = "year",       # quoted: this column is being created
    values_to = "estimate"   # quoted: this column is being created
  )

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  county year  estimate
  <chr>  <chr>    <dbl>
1 Alder  2021      10.1
2 Alder  2022      10.4
3 Alder  2023      10.2
4 Birch  2021      12  
5 Birch  2022      12.3
6 Birch  2023      12.5


Arguments:

cols: which existing columns to stack
names_to: name of the new column that holds the old column names
values_to: name of the new column that holds the cell values



In class, the Ted Lasso data had one row and columns like F_count_RK_S1_e1 (Roy Kent’s count, season 1, episode 1) and F_count_total_S1_e1. names_pattern uses a regular expression to pull the pieces apart:

tl_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("F_count_"),
    names_to = c(".value", "Season", "Episode"),
    names_pattern = "F_count_(RK|total)_S(\\d+)_e(\\d+)"
  )


Each ( ) group in the pattern fills one entry of names_to

Group 1, (RK|total): “RK” or “total”
Group 2, S(\\d+): the digits after S, i.e. the season
Group 3, e(\\d+): the digits after e, i.e. the episode

".value" is special: instead of making a column called .value, the matched text (RK, total) becomes column names, so the result has one row per episode with an RK column and a total column
\\d+ means “one or more digits” (regex cheat sheet: the stringr regex vignette)





Use when one case is spread across several rows (e.g. CDC PLACES has one row per county per measure).

long <- tribble(
  ~county, ~measure,   ~value,
  "Alder", "Diabetes", 10.2,
  "Alder", "Obesity",  31.0,
  "Birch", "Diabetes", 12.5,
  "Birch", "Obesity",  33.4
)

long |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = county,        # one row per county
    names_from = measure,    # new column names come from here
    values_from = value      # cell values come from here
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  county Diabetes Obesity
  <chr>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Alder      10.2    31  
2 Birch      12.5    33.4



names_from can take several columns, e.g. names_from = c(MeasureId, Data_Value_Type), which glues them into names like DIABETES_Crude prevalence




The raw class survey had free-text answers like "45 minutes", "1 hr", and "30" in a minutes column. Write the cleaning steps in order before coding:
Pseudocode:

Make everything lowercase so "Hr" and "hr" match
Find the answers given in hours with str_detect()
Pull out the number with parse_number()
Multiply the hour answers by 60
Check what’s left with count() and decide what to do with anything unusable (set to NA, don’t guess)

Code Implementation:

survey <- tibble(routine_min = c("45 minutes", "1 hr", "30", "1.5 hours", "idk"))

Question: In a standard 52-card deck, give every card a point value:

deck <- read_csv("data/card_deck.csv")
